paragraphs: The charioteer then swung his horses around toward the ships, and they raced ahead willingly. Foam whitened their chests and dust whitened their bellies as they carried the wounded king out of the battle.

Hector saw Agamemnon leave the field, and he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians. “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanian warriors, be men, my friends, and fight bravely. Their best man has left them, and Zeus has granted me a great triumph. Drive your chariots at the enemy, and win still greater glory.”

Those words put heart and soul into every one of them. A huntsman sets his dogs on a lion or a wild boar, and in the same way Hector, the equal of Ares, set the proud Trojans on the Achaeans. Full of hope, he plunged in among the foremost fighters. He fell on the battle like a fierce storm that swoops down on the sea and whips its deep blue waters into a fury.

Who, then, were all those that Hector son of Priam killed in the hour of triumph that Zeus gave him? First Asaeus, Autonous, and Opites; Dolops son of Clytius, Opheltius and Agelaus; Aesymnus, Orus and Hipponous, steadfast in battle. These were the Achaean chieftains Hector killed, and then he fell on the rank and file. It was like the west wind shoving the clouds of the white south and beating them down in its fury: the waves of the sea roll high, and the spray is flung up in the rage of the wandering wind. In just that way the heads of the men who fell by Hector’s hand lay thick.

Everything would have been lost then, with no remedy, and the Achaeans would have fled in a jumble to their ships, if Odysseus had not called out to Diomedes. “Son of Tydeus, what has come over us, that we forget our fighting strength? Come, my good fellow, stand beside me and help me. We will be shamed forever if Hector takes the ships.”
Diomedes answered, “I will hold my ground, whatever comes. But we will get little joy from it, because Zeus wants to give victory to the Trojans rather than to us.”

With these words Diomedes knocked Thymbraeus from his chariot to the ground, driving his spear into his left breast. Odysseus killed Molion, who was his squire. They left these two lying there, since the pair had ended their fighting. The two heroes then went on wreaking havoc on the enemy, like two wild boars that wheel around in fury and tear the hounds hunting them. So they turned on the Trojans and killed them, and the Achaeans were grateful for a breathing space in their flight from Hector.

Next they took two princes along with their chariot: the two sons of Merops of Percote, who surpassed all other men in the art of divination. He had forbidden his sons to go to the war, but they did not obey him, because fate was luring them to their deaths. Diomedes son of Tydeus killed them both and stripped them of their armor, while Odysseus killed Hippodamus and Hypeirochus.

Now the son of Cronus, looking down from Ida, ordained that neither side should gain the advantage, and they kept on killing one another. The son of Tydeus speared Agastrophus son of Paeon in the hip joint. Agastrophus had no chariot at hand to escape in, so blindly confident had he been. His squire was holding it some distance away, while he fought on foot among the foremost until he lost his life. Hector soon noticed the havoc Diomedes and Odysseus were causing. He bore down on them with a loud cry, and the Trojan ranks followed him. Brave Diomedes was dismayed at the sight and said to Odysseus beside him, “Great Hector is bearing down on us, and we will be undone. Let us stand firm and wait for his attack.”

He poised his spear as he spoke and hurled it, and he did not miss his mark. He had aimed at Hector’s head near the top of the helmet, but bronze was turned by bronze. The spear was stopped by the visored helmet of three metal plates that Phoebus Apollo had given Hector, and Hector was untouched. He sprang back with a great bound under cover of the ranks. He fell on his knees and propped himself up with his brawny hand on the ground, because darkness had fallen over his eyes. The son of Tydeus, having thrown his spear, dashed in among the foremost fighters to where he had seen it strike the ground. Meanwhile Hector recovered, sprang back into his chariot, and mingled with the crowd, and so he saved his life. But Diomedes came at him with his spear and said, “Dog, you have got away again, though death was close on your heels. Phoebus Apollo, to whom I think you pray before you go into battle, has saved you again. Still, I will meet you and make an end of you later, if any god will stand by me too and help me. For now I must go after the ones I can lay hands on.”

While he spoke, Diomedes began stripping the spoils from the son of Paeon. But Paris, husband of lovely Helen, was leaning against a pillar of the monument that men had raised long ago to Ilus son of Dardanus, a ruler in days of old, and from there he aimed an arrow at him. Diomedes had taken the cuirass from Agastrophus’s breast, along with his heavy helmet and the shield from his shoulders, when Paris drew his bow and let fly an arrow. It did not leave his hand in vain. It pierced the flat of Diomedes’s right foot, went right through it, and fixed itself in the ground. Paris sprang out from his hiding place with a hearty laugh and taunted him. “You are wounded—my arrow was not shot in vain. I wish it had hit you in the belly and killed you. Then the Trojans, who fear you as goats fear a lion, would have had a break from their misery.”

Diomedes answered, quite undaunted, “Archer, you are nothing without your bow. Slanderer, seducer! If you were tried in single combat, fighting in full armor, your bow and arrows would do you little good. Your boast is empty, just because you have scratched the sole of my foot. I care no more than if a girl or some silly boy had hit me. A worthless coward can inflict only a light wound. When I wound a man, even if I only graze his skin, it is another matter, because my weapon lays him low. His wife will tear her cheeks in grief and his children will be fatherless. He will rot there, reddening the earth with his blood, and vultures, not women, will gather around him.”

So he spoke, and Odysseus came up and stood over him. Under this cover Diomedes sat down and drew the arrow from his foot, and the pain was sharp as he did it. Then he sprang onto his chariot and told the charioteer to drive him to the ships, for he was sick at heart.

Odysseus was now alone. Not one of the Argives stood by him, because panic had seized them all. “Alas,” he said to himself in dismay, “what will become of me? It is bad if I turn and run from these odds, but worse if I am left alone and taken prisoner, since the son of Cronus has struck the rest of the Danaans with panic. But why do I talk to myself like this? I know well that cowards quit the field, while a hero, whether he wounds or is wounded, must stand firm and hold his own.”

While he was torn between two choices, the Trojan ranks advanced and closed around him, and they would bitterly regret it. It was as when hounds and strong young men set upon a wild boar that charges out of his lair, whetting his white tusks. They attack him from every side and hear his jaws gnashing, yet for all his fierceness they hold their ground. In the same way the Trojans furiously attacked Odysseus. First he sprang at Deiopites, spear in hand, and wounded him on the shoulder with a downward blow. Then he killed Thoon and Ennomus. After these he struck Chersidamas in the loins, under his shield, as the man had just leapt down from his chariot. Chersidamas fell in the dust and clutched the earth in the hollow of his hand. Odysseus left these men lying and went on to wound Charops son of Hippasus, own brother to noble Socus. Socus, hero that he was, hurried to help his brother. When he was close to Odysseus he said, “Far-famed Odysseus, insatiable for craft and toil, today you will either boast of killing both sons of Hippasus and stripping them of their armor, or you will fall to my spear.”

With these words Socus struck the shield of Odysseus. The spear went through the shield and on through his richly wrought cuirass, tearing the flesh from his side, but Pallas Athena did not let it pierce the hero’s entrails. Odysseus knew that his hour had not yet come. He gave ground and said to Socus, “Wretch, now you will surely die. You have kept me from fighting further against the Trojans, but you will fall to my spear, giving glory to me and your soul to Hades of the noble horses.”

Socus had turned to run, but as he did, the spear struck him in the back midway between the shoulders and went right through his chest. He fell heavily to the ground, and Odysseus boasted over him. “Socus, son of Hippasus, tamer of horses, death has been too quick for you, and you have not escaped it. Poor wretch, not even in death will your father and mother close your eyes. The ravening vultures will cover you with the flapping of their dark wings and devour you. But if I fall, the Achaeans will give me the proper rites of burial.”

With that, Odysseus drew Socus’s heavy spear out of his flesh and out of his shield. The blood welled out when the spear was pulled free, and that dismayed him badly. When the Trojans saw that Odysseus was bleeding, they raised a great shout and came at him in a body. He gave ground and called to his comrades to come help him. Three times he cried as loudly as a man can, and three times brave Menelaus heard him. Menelaus turned to Ajax, who was close beside him, and said, “Ajax, noble son of Telamon, captain of your people, the cry of Odysseus rings in my ears, as though the Trojans had cut him off and were getting the better of him, alone as he is. Let us make our way through the throng and defend him. I fear he may come to harm, for all his valor, if he is left without support, and the Danaans would miss him badly.”

Menelaus led the way, and mighty Ajax went with him. The Trojans had gathered around Odysseus like ravenous mountain jackals around the carcass of a horned stag that has been hit with an arrow. The stag runs at full speed as long as his blood is warm and his strength lasts; when the arrow overcomes him, the savage jackals devour him in the shady glades of the forest. Then heaven sends a fierce lion their way, the jackals run in terror, and the lion robs them of their prey. In the same way many brave Trojans gathered around crafty Odysseus, but the hero stood at bay and kept them off with his spear. Then Ajax came up with his shield before him like a wall and stood close by, and the Trojans fled in all directions. Menelaus took Odysseus by the hand and led him out of the press while his squire brought up his chariot. Ajax rushed furiously at the Trojans and killed Doryclus, a bastard son of Priam. Then he wounded Pandocus, Lysandrus, Pyrasus, and Pylartes. Ajax was like a swollen torrent that rushes in full flood from the mountains onto the plain, big with the rain of heaven. It engulfs many a dry oak and many a pine, and it brings down much mud and casts it into the sea. So brave Ajax chased the enemy furiously over the plain, slaying men and horses alike.

Hector did not yet know what Ajax was doing. He was fighting on the far left of the battle by the banks of the river Scamander, where the slaughter was thickest and the war cry loudest around Nestor and brave Idomeneus. Hector was making great slaughter among them with his spear and furious driving, destroying the ranks that stood against him. Even so, the Achaeans would not have given ground if Paris, husband of lovely Helen, had not stopped the prowess of Machaon, shepherd of his people, by wounding him in the right shoulder with a triple-barbed arrow. The Achaeans were in great fear that, with the fight turned against them, the Trojans might take Machaon prisoner. Idomeneus said to Nestor, “Nestor son of Neleus, honor of the Achaean name, get into your chariot at once. Take Machaon with you and drive your horses to the ships as fast as you can. A physician is worth more than several other men put together, because he can cut out arrows and spread healing herbs.”

Nestor, knight of Gerene, did as Idomeneus had advised. He got into his chariot at once, and Machaon, son of the famed physician Asclepius, went with him. Nestor lashed the horses, and they flew toward the ships without hesitation, as if of their own free will.

Then Cebriones saw the Trojans in confusion and spoke to Hector from his place beside him. “Hector, the two of us are fighting out here on the far wing of the battle, while the other Trojans are in a jumbled rout, themselves and their horses. Ajax son of Telamon is driving them before him. I know him by the breadth of his shield. Let us turn our chariot and horses to where horse and foot are fighting hardest and the battle cry is loudest.”

Cebriones lashed his fine horses. They felt the whip and pulled the chariot at full speed into the Achaeans and Trojans, over the bodies and shields of the fallen. Blood spattered the axle, and the rail around the car was covered with splashes thrown up by the horses’ hoofs and the tires of the wheels. Hector tore his way through and flung himself into the thick of the fight. The Danaans fell into confusion when he appeared, since his spear was never idle for long. He went among the ranks with sword and spear and threw great stones, yet he kept clear of Ajax son of Telamon, because Zeus would have been angry if Hector had fought a better man than himself.

Then father Zeus on his high throne struck fear into the heart of Ajax. Ajax stood there dazed and threw his shield behind him. He looked fearfully at the throng of his enemies like some wild beast, turning this way and that but backing away slowly, crouching. It was like peasants and their hounds driving a lion from their stockyard and keeping watch by night to stop him carrying off the pick of their herd. He makes his greedy spring, but in vain, for darts from many a strong hand fall thick around him, and burning brands scare him for all his fury, and when morning comes he slinks away, foiled and angry. In the same way Ajax, sorely against his will, retreated angrily before the Trojans, fearing for the ships of the Achaeans. Or he was like a lazy ass that has had many a cudgel broken on his back. He goes into a field and starts eating the corn. Boys beat him, but he is too much for them, and though they lay about with their sticks they cannot hurt him. Still, when he has had his fill, they finally drive him from the field. In the same way the Trojans and their allies pursued great Ajax, ever striking the middle of his shield with their darts. Now and again he would turn and show fight, holding back the Trojan battalions, and then he would retreat again. But he kept any of them from making his way to the ships. He stood alone midway between the Trojans and Achaeans. Of the spears that sped from their hands, some stuck in his mighty shield, while many fell to the ground, though thirsting for his blood, before they could reach him and wound his fair flesh.
